entries.type: correlative (the split form of the quasi-coordinator as well as; the first as is a degree adverb and well an adverb, so only the second as is the conjunction — unsplit, the same three words are also the equative of she plays as well as her brother)
entries.register: archaic; survives in legal and older literary prose
entries.clause: coordinate elements — joins noun phrases, prepositional phrases, and adjectives
entries.pattern: as well [X] as [Y] · as well [prepositional phrase] as [prepositional phrase] · [verb] as well [object] as [object] · as well [subject] as [subject] + plural verb · as well [adjective] as [adjective]
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves. The commas that fence the modern as well as when it interrupts a subject and its verb (The manager, as well as the interns, was invited) have no equivalent here, because the split frame coordinates the two items instead of adding one parenthetically.
entries.meaning: The old split arrangement of as well as: the well stays with the first item and the second as introduces the other, so as well the rich as the poor means both of them. Because both items sit inside the frame it coordinates like both … and, where the modern unsplit as well as leaves the first item grammatically in charge and the verb singular. Nothing but fossilized phrasing survives in current American English — write both X and Y or X as well as Y.
examples: The statute binds as well the buyer as the seller.
The fire took as well the barn as the house.
He was remembered as well for his temper as for his generosity.
As well the officers as the men were paid out of the same fund.
The collection holds letters as well in French as in English.
The charter protected as well those born in the town as those who settled there later.

entries.type: correlative (at once is elsewhere an adverb of time meaning "immediately" — come at once; the and half is the ordinary coordinator)
entries.clause: coordinate elements — most often two adjectives or two noun phrases in predicate position
entries.pattern: [subject] + be + at once [adjective] and [adjective] · at once [noun phrase] and [noun phrase] · [verb] at once [X] and [Y] · at once [adjective], [adjective], and [adjective] (three or more) · at once both [X] and [Y]
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves in the two-item form. With three or more items, punctuate the run as an ordinary series: at once cheap, fast, and reliable.
entries.meaning: Says that both descriptions hold simultaneously, and usually implies they sit oddly together — at once familiar and strange. It is the literary cousin of both … and, and the temporal reading of at once ("immediately") drops away as soon as the and half arrives.
examples: The house was at once grand and uninhabitable.
Her answer was at once polite and devastating.
The book is at once a memoir and a history of the town.
He managed to be at once the funniest person in the room and the loneliest.
The ruling is at once narrow and far-reaching.
The score is at once cheap, fast, and impossible to argue with.

entries.type: correlative (both on its own is a determiner and a pronoun — both books, both of them; the and half is the ordinary coordinator of bread and butter)
entries.clause: coordinate elements — joins words, phrases, and matching subordinate clauses, but not two independent clauses
entries.pattern: both [X] and [Y] (X and Y the same kind of element) · both [subject] and [subject] + plural verb · [subject] both [verb phrase] and [verb phrase] · [verb] both [object] and [object] · both [prepositional phrase] and [prepositional phrase] · both [subordinate clause] and [subordinate clause] (both that he knew and that he said nothing)
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves — never both the coach, and the players. Since it joins phrases rather than clauses, a comma before this and is almost always an error.
variants: both … as well as (nonstandard blend; use both X and Y, or X as well as Y)
entries.meaning: Adds two things together and puts emphasis on the fact that there are two — plain and reports the pair, both … and insists on it. It takes exactly two elements, and unlike either … or, a both … and subject always takes a plural verb.
examples: She speaks both Spanish and Portuguese at home.
Both the coach and the players were fined.
The apartment is both cheaper and closer to campus.
He both wrote the score and conducted the premiere.
We ate both before the movie and after it.
The bill has both Republican and Democratic sponsors.

entries.type: correlative (either on its own is a determiner, a pronoun, and a negative-echo adverb — either way, I don't either; the or half is the ordinary coordinator)
entries.clause: coordinate elements, or two coordinate independent clauses
entries.pattern: either [X] or [Y] · either [subject] or [subject] + verb agreeing with the nearer one · [subject] either [verb phrase] or [verb phrase] · [verb] either [object] or [object] · [subject] + be + either [complement] or [complement] · Either [independent clause], or [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves when they join words or phrases. Put a comma before or only when it joins two independent clauses: Either you tell him, or I will. Two short imperatives sharing one understood subject count as coordinated verb phrases rather than clauses, so they take no comma: Either finish the report or hand it off.
variants: either … or else (informal, adds a threat)
or … or (archaic and poetic — the either dropped and the coordinator doubled instead: or by force or by guile)
entries.meaning: Offers two alternatives and asserts that one of them holds. Against plain or, the either warns the listener in advance that a choice is coming and closes the list at two. The verb agrees with whichever subject stands nearer to it, which is the difference that trips learners up: Either the twins or Maria is driving.
examples: We can either drive or take the train.
Either the twins or Maria is driving tonight.
Either you tell him, or I will.
The paint comes in either matte or gloss.
She's either brilliant or completely reckless.
Either finish the report or hand it off — I don't care which.

entries.type: correlative (neither on its own is a determiner, a pronoun, and an adverb — neither one, me neither; nor is also a plain coordinator)
entries.clause: coordinate elements, or two coordinate independent clauses
entries.pattern: neither [X] nor [Y] · neither [subject] nor [subject] + verb agreeing with the nearer one · [subject] neither [verb phrase] nor [verb phrase] · [subject] + be + neither [complement] nor [complement] · [verb] neither [object] nor [object] · Neither [independent clause], nor [inverted independent clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between short paired elements. Use a comma before nor when it joins two independent clauses, each of which then inverts: Neither did he call, nor did he write.
variants: nor … nor (literary and archaic — the neither dropped and the coordinator doubled instead: nor rain nor snow)
entries.meaning: Denies both alternatives at once; it is the exact negative of both … and. The pair already carries the negation, so the verb stays positive — Neither of them was invited, never wasn't invited. Everyday American speech usually reaches for not … or instead and saves neither … nor for writing.
examples: Neither the manager nor the assistants were told about the merger.
He neither apologized nor offered to pay for the window.
The soup was neither hot nor cold.
Neither Maria nor the twins are driving.
She neither confirmed nor denied the report.
Neither rain nor snow keeps her off that trail.
Neither did he call, nor did he write.

entries.respell: NOR … NOR, nur (the doubled form is rhetorical, so both halves normally keep full stress; only in running prose does the first flatten)
entries.type: correlative (both halves are the ordinary coordinator nor, the one FANBOYS member that carries its own negation; the same nor is the second half of neither … nor and the clause coordinator of He didn't call, nor did he write)
entries.register: archaic and poetic — an American meets it in Shakespeare, the King James Bible, hymn texts, and nineteenth-century verse, and essentially nowhere else
entries.clause: coordinate elements — joins noun phrases, adjectives, and prepositional phrases, all of them negated
entries.pattern: nor [X] nor [Y] · nor [subject] nor [subject] + verb agreeing with the nearer one · [verb] nor [object] nor [object] · [subject] + be + nor [complement] nor [complement] · nor [X], nor [Y], nor [Z] (extended run)
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves in a two-item pair. Older printing commas every item in a longer run — nor brass, nor stone, nor earth — and that is the style to copy in period voice. The negation sits in the nor itself, so the verb stays positive: nor gold nor threat could move him, never couldn't move him.
entries.meaning: The neither dropped and the coordinator doubled in its place, so the opening nor does the announcing that neither normally does. The meaning is identical to neither … nor; only the register differs, and it differs enormously — this is verse and scripture, not a choice available in modern writing. Agreement follows the same rule as its modern twin: the verb matches whichever subject stands nearer to it.
examples: Nor gold nor threat could move him from his purpose.
Nor sun nor star was seen for three days together.
There is nor peace nor profit in that quarrel.
Nor the captain nor his officers were ashore that night.
Nor by force nor by persuasion would the old woman give up the deed.
The wind spared nor roof, nor rick, nor fence along the whole valley.
Nor death nor life shall part us from that love.

entries.type: correlative (but is also a plain coordinator and a preposition meaning "except" — everyone but me)
entries.clause: coordinate elements — corrective coordination
entries.pattern: not [X] but [Y] · [subject] [verb] not [X] but [Y] · [subject] + be + not [X] but [Y] · not [X] but rather [Y] · not because [clause] but because [clause] · not to [verb] but to [verb] · not that [clause] but that [clause]
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves when the elements are short. A comma before but is acceptable, and common, when the elements run long or the contrast is being pointed: It wasn't the heat, but the humidity.
entries.meaning: Rejects one description and substitutes the correct one, so the weight of the sentence lands on the second half. Plain but adds a contrasting fact; not … but replaces — the first element is denied outright rather than qualified.
examples: That was not a request but an order.
He came not to argue but to listen.
The problem is not the price but the delivery time.
She's not angry, but disappointed.
We canceled not because the numbers were bad but because the timing was wrong.
The best players are not the strongest but the most patient.

entries.type: correlative (but is also a plain coordinator; also is a mobile adverb, which is why it can slide down the second half or surface as as well or too)
entries.clause: coordinate elements, or two coordinate independent clauses
entries.pattern: [subject] not only [verb phrase] but also [verb phrase] · not only [noun phrase] but also [noun phrase] · [subject] + be + not only [complement] but also [complement] · not only [subject] but also [subject] + verb agreeing with the nearer one · Not only [auxiliary] [subject] [verb], but [subject] also [verb] · Not only [auxiliary] [subject] [verb], but [clause] as well.
entries.punctuation: No comma inside the pair when it joins phrases. When not only is fronted and the clause inverts, put a comma before but: Not only did he apologize, but he also sent flowers.
entries.meaning: Adds a second item and flags it as the more surprising or more important of the two, so the sentence builds toward the but also half. Fronting not only forces subject-auxiliary inversion the way any fronted negative does; leaving it mid-sentence does not. Like either … or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
examples: He wants not only a raise but also a corner office.
Not only did she apologize, but she sent flowers as well.
The storm not only flooded the basement but also took out the fence.
Not only is the software free, but it runs on almost anything.
She's not just a good writer but a fast one.
Not only the players but also the coach was fined.

entries.type: correlative (as on its own is a preposition — as a teacher — and a subordinator of time, reason, and manner)
entries.clause: coordinate elements — corrective comparison
entries.pattern: [subject] + be + not so much [X] as [Y] · [subject] [verb] not so much [phrase] as [phrase] · not so much [prepositional phrase] as [prepositional phrase] · not so much because [clause] as because [clause] · It's not so much that [clause] as that [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves; a comma before as is optional and marks emphasis.
entries.meaning: Says the second description fits better than the first without throwing the first out entirely. It is the softened cousin of not … but, which rejects the first element flatly.
examples: It's not so much a complaint as an observation.
He was not so much angry as embarrassed.
The trouble is not so much that she's late as that she never calls.
What sank the deal was not so much the price as the deadline.
She sang the last line not so much to the audience as to herself.
They lost not so much because the defense collapsed as because they kept giving the ball away.

entries.respell: OR … OR, er (both halves take full stress in verse; in running speech the second flattens to er)
entries.type: correlative (both halves are the ordinary coordinator or; the first or simply stands where either would in the modern pair, which is why nothing else in the sentence has to change)
entries.register: archaic and poetic — Elizabethan drama, Milton, hymn texts, and nineteenth-century verse; in modern American prose it reads either as a typo or as costume
entries.clause: coordinate elements, or two coordinate independent clauses
entries.pattern: or [X] or [Y] · or [prepositional phrase] or [prepositional phrase] · or [subject] or [subject] + verb agreeing with the nearer one · [subject] [modal] or [bare infinitive] or [bare infinitive] · Or [independent clause], or [independent clause]. · or [X], or [Y], or [Z] (extended run)
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves when they join words or phrases. Put a comma before the second or when it joins two independent clauses, exactly as with either … or, and comma an extended run throughout.
entries.meaning: The positive twin of nor … nor: the either is dropped and the coordinator itself doubles, so the opening or is what warns that a choice is coming. It asserts exactly what either … or asserts and differs only in register — or by force or by guile is period voice, and outside pastiche modern American English has no use for it. Like its modern twin it closes the list at two unless the run is deliberately extended.
examples: Or by force or by guile, the town would be taken before winter.
He must or sell the land or mortgage it.
Or king or commoner, the fever made no distinction.
She would have her answer or tonight or never.
Or the sergeant or his men were lying, and the court meant to learn which.
The word will come or by rider or by post, but come it will.
Or fight or flee — there was no third road out of that valley.

entries.respell: WEH-thur … OR, er (a homophone of weather for most Americans)
entries.type: correlative (whether is the rare half with no second job — it is only ever a subordinator; contrast if, which is both a conditional subordinator and a complementizer. The or half is the ordinary coordinator)
entries.clause: noun clause (indirect question); with or not, an adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: [verb] whether [clause] or [clause] · [verb] whether [X] or [Y] · [preposition] whether [clause] or [clause] · whether to [verb] or [verb] · Whether [clause] or not, [main clause]. · [main clause] whether [clause] or not.
entries.punctuation: No comma inside the pair. When a concessive whether … or … clause opens the sentence, close it with a comma: Whether you like it or not, we're going. When the same clause trails the main clause, no comma: We're going whether you like it or not. A whether noun clause never takes a comma in either position.
entries.meaning: Lays out two possibilities without choosing between them. As a noun clause it names an open question; with or not it turns concessive, meaning both possibilities lead to the same result. Unlike if, whether can follow a preposition, take to + infinitive, and open a sentence — whether to go, never if to go.
examples: I can't tell whether he's serious or joking.
Whether you like it or not, the deadline stands.
She hasn't decided whether to fly or drive.
It depends on whether the permit clears or the city stalls again.
Ask him whether the store opens at eight or nine.
Whether or not they call back, I'm taking the other offer.
He'll say something at the meeting whether anyone asks him or not.

entries.type: correlative frame (both halves are prepositional phrases used as sentence adverbials, not conjunctions; for is elsewhere a preposition and the causal coordinator of the FANBOYS)
entries.clause: none — each half is a sentence adverbial standing in front of its own independent clause
entries.pattern: For one thing, [clause]. For another, [clause]. · For one thing, [clause]; for another, [clause]. · For one thing, [clause]. For another thing, [clause]. And for a third, [clause]. · [clause] — for one thing [clause], for another [clause] · For one thing, [clause]. (second half never supplied)
entries.punctuation: A comma after each half, separating it from the clause it introduces. Between the two clauses use a period or a semicolon — a comma alone leaves a splice, since both halves are adverbials and neither one joins anything.
variants: for one thing … for another thing
entries.meaning: Enumerates reasons for a judgment already announced, and claims by its shape that there is more than one. It is the conversational alternative to first … second, and the second half is often never supplied at all — for one thing on its own already promises a list.
examples: For one thing, the rent is too high. For another, the commute runs an hour each way.
I wouldn't buy that car — for one thing it's out of warranty, for another the parts take weeks.
For one thing, nobody asked us; for another, nobody paid us.
She'd never last as a line cook: for one thing, she hates crowds; for another, she can't stand the heat.
For one thing, the data is two years old. For another thing, half the responses came from one county.
He shouldn't be driving. For one thing, he can't read the signs anymore.
related: on the one hand … on the other hand

entries.type: correlative frame (both halves are the time adverb now in an old distributive sense, "at one moment"; neither is a conjunction, which is why a coordinator can sit between them — now hot, now cold or now hot and now cold)
entries.clause: none — it pairs two adverbials, adjectives, or parallel clauses describing alternating states
entries.pattern: now [adjective], now [adjective] · now [verb phrase], now [verb phrase] · now [clause], now [clause] · now [X], now [Y], now [Z] (extended alternation) · now [X] and now [Y]
entries.punctuation: Comma between the halves — the pair reads as a list of alternating states, not as a joined phrase. Where the halves are full clauses, use a semicolon.
variants: at one moment … at the next
entries.meaning: Marks a state that keeps switching back and forth: at one moment this, at the next that. The now here has nothing to do with present time — it is a distributive survival that lives on in poetry and heightened prose, and it should not be confused with the causal and temporal subordinator now that.
examples: The wind was now at our backs, now in our faces.
She played the part now as comedy, now as tragedy.
The river runs now fast, now slow, depending on the month.
His voice rose and fell, now a whisper, now a shout.
The lamp swung over the water, now bright, now almost gone.
Prices climbed all winter, now by pennies and now by dollars.

entries.term: on the one hand … on the other hand
entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈwʌn hænd/ … /ɑn ði ˈʌðər hænd/
entries.type: correlative frame (both halves are prepositional phrases working as conjunctive adverbs, not conjunctions; the second half has a full independent life without the first)
entries.register: neutral, at home in essays and analysis
entries.clause: none — each half is a sentence adverbial in front of its own independent clause
entries.pattern: On the one hand, [clause]; on the other hand, [clause]. · On the one hand, [clause]. On the other, [clause]. · On the one hand [noun phrase], on the other [noun phrase] · [clause]; on the other hand, [clause]. (first half dropped) · On the one hand, [clause]; but on the other, [clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma after each half. Between the two clauses use a semicolon or a period — a comma alone is a splice, exactly as with however. Mind the article, which does not match across the halves: the one hand but the other hand.
variants: on the one hand … on the other
on one hand … on the other hand (informal, the first the dropped)
on the one hand … but then again
entries.meaning: Lays out two sides of a question and weighs them against each other, framing an argument rather than joining grammatical elements. It is the one pair in the file whose halves are unequal in independence: on the other hand is a standard conjunctive adverb that needs no setup, while a first half with nothing after it leaves the reader waiting.
examples: On the one hand, the rent is cheap; on the other hand, the commute is brutal.
On the one hand she wanted the promotion; on the other, she dreaded the travel.
On the one hand, the drug works. On the other, almost nobody can afford it.
The plan saves money. On the other hand, it costs us a month.
On the one hand, the numbers look strong; on the other hand, they come from a single quarter.
On the one hand a bigger kitchen, on the other a longer drive — we took the kitchen.

entries.type: correlative frame (both halves are bare noun phrases used adverbially, the same construction as this morning; neither half is a conjunction)
entries.clause: none — each half is a time adverbial fronting its own clause
entries.pattern: One minute [clause], the next [clause]. · One minute [X], the next [Y]. (both verbs dropped) · One minute [clause] and the next [clause]. · One second / one moment / one day [clause], the next [clause]. · One minute [clause]; the next, [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma between the halves. Both halves front independent clauses, so careful writing upgrades that comma to a semicolon or a dash when the clauses run long; the plain comma survives in speech-like prose.
entries.meaning: Reports a sudden switch between two states, with the shortness of the named interval doing all the emphasis. It is the everyday counterpart of literary now … now, and unlike a plain sequence it always implies the change was abrupt or out of character.
examples: One minute the sun was out, the next it was pouring.
One minute he's your best friend, the next he won't answer a text.
One minute the server was fine; the next, half the site was down.
One day the store was busy, the next it was closed for good.
One moment she was laughing, the next she was in tears.
The market gave it all back — one minute we were up eight percent, the next we were flat.

entries.type: correlative frame (both halves are the ordinary degree adverb partly; nothing here is a conjunction, and a coordinator between the halves is optional)
entries.clause: none — it pairs two adjuncts, most often two because clauses or two prepositional phrases of cause
entries.pattern: partly [X], partly [Y] · partly because [clause], partly because [clause] · partly [prepositional phrase] and partly [prepositional phrase] · partly [adjective], partly [adjective] · partly [X], partly [Y], and partly [Z] (three or more shares)
entries.punctuation: Comma between the halves, since the second partly opens a fresh adjunct rather than a second element of one phrase: partly because of the weather, partly because of the cost. With and between the halves the comma is optional.
variants: half … half (informal: half amused, half annoyed)
entries.meaning: Splits a cause, a description, or a composition into two shares, neither of which accounts for the whole. That is the difference from both … and, which asserts two complete facts: partly … partly concedes in advance that each half is only some of the story.
examples: The delay was partly our fault, partly the weather.
She took the job partly because it paid more, partly because it was closer to home.
The wall is partly brick and partly plaster.
His expression was partly amusement, partly alarm.
The shortage is partly a supply problem and partly a pricing one.
The trip was partly research, partly vacation, and partly an excuse to see her sister.
related: on the one hand … on the other hand

entries.respell: AZ … AZ (both halves usually flatten to uhz in running speech)
entries.type: correlative (the first as is a degree adverb, the second the subordinator; as on its own is also a preposition — as a teacher — and a subordinator of time, reason, and manner)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison, usually elliptical
entries.pattern: as [adjective/adverb] as [noun phrase] · as [adjective/adverb] as [clause] · as [adjective] a(n) [singular noun] as [noun phrase] · as many/much [noun] as [noun phrase] · not as [adjective] as [noun phrase] · As [adjective/adverb] as [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair. But when the whole as … as stretch is a fronted adverbial clause, close it with a comma at the seam, like any other fronted subordinate clause: As soon as the door closed, everyone started talking. Sitting in its ordinary place after the main clause it takes none: Everyone started talking as soon as the door closed.
entries.meaning: States equality of degree: the first as is a degree adverb, the second is the conjunction that introduces the standard. Where more … than ranks one thing above another, as … as levels them. One trap in the noun pattern: with a singular count noun the article jumps to the far side of the adjective — as good a manager as, never as a good manager as.
examples: The sequel is as good as the original.
Call me as soon as you land.
It didn't cost as much as I expected.
She works as hard as anyone on the floor.
Get here as early as you can.
He's as tall as his father is now.
She's as good a manager as the company has ever had.
As soon as the door closed, everyone started talking.

entries.respell: AZ, uhz … ee-vun-SOH (the opening as is unstressed and normally reduces; the weight of the sentence lands on so)
entries.type: correlative (only the first half is a conjunction — as is elsewhere a preposition and a subordinator of time, reason, and manner; even so is the resumptive adverb so with an intensifier in front of it, which is why it can shrink to bare so without changing the grammar)
entries.register: archaic and biblical — the register of the King James Bible, of hymn texts, and of pulpit and platform oratory in the older style
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison, fronted, with the main clause following even so
entries.pattern: As [clause], even so [main clause]. · As [clause], even so [verb] [subject]. (inverted main clause) · As [noun phrase], even so [main clause]. (verbless first half) · Just as [clause], even so [main clause]. · As [clause], even so also [main clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma between the halves is required — the fronted as clause has to close before even so opens the main clause. Never a comma after even so here, and that is the fastest way to tell the pair from its look-alike: the free-standing conjunctive adverb even so does take one (Even so, we went) and needs a semicolon or a period in front of it, because it links two independent clauses instead of finishing a comparison.
variants: even as … so (the same emphasis moved to the first half)
entries.meaning: The emphatic form of as … so: even leans on the so and insists the second case matches the first point for point, where plain so merely draws the parallel. It is how scripture and the preaching built on it make an analogy, and outside that world — sermons, hymnody, older oratory, deliberate pastiche — an American will not meet it. Do not confuse the paired even so with the free-standing conjunctive adverb even so, which concedes what came before and then holds out against it rather than matching it.
examples: As the sparks fly upward, even so man is born to trouble.
As the rain returns not to the cloud, even so the word goes not out in vain.
As the seed is sown, even so shall the harvest be.
As the body without the spirit is dead, even so is faith without works.
As the vine is pruned that it may bear, even so is a people chastened that it may endure.
As the fathers bore the heat of the day, even so must this generation bear it.
As the republic was founded in argument, even so will it be preserved by argument.

entries.type: correlative (as much as is also a fixed concessive subordinator meaning "although," and an adverbial of approximation — as much as $400)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison (quantity or degree), often elliptical
entries.pattern: as much [uncountable noun] as [noun phrase] · as many [countable noun] as [noun phrase] · [verb] as much as [clause] · not as much [noun] as [noun phrase] · As much as [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair. When as much as opens a concessive clause, close that clause with a comma: As much as I like him, I wouldn't hire him.
entries.meaning: The quantity version of as … as: as much with uncountable nouns, as many with countable ones. It has a second life as a fixed concessive, where as much as I'd love to simply means although I'd love to.
examples: We don't have as much time as we thought.
She earns as much now as both her parents did.
There weren't as many people as last year.
He complained as much as everyone else did.
As much as I like the neighborhood, I can't afford it.
Take as much cake as you want.

entries.respell: JUST-az … SOH (the stress sits on just, not on as)
entries.type: correlative (so is also a coordinator — I was tired, so I left — a degree adverb, and a pro-form standing in for a whole clause: I think so)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison
entries.pattern: Just as [clause], so [clause]. · Just as [clause], so too [clause]. · Just as [clause], so [verb] [subject]. (inverted second half) · As [clause], so [clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma between the halves is required — the just as clause is fronted and has to be closed off before so begins the main clause.
variants: as … even so (biblical and emphatic: as the sparks fly upward, even so man is born to trouble)
entries.meaning: Sets up a proportion: what holds in the first situation holds in the same way in the second. It is the pulpit-and-essay relative of the … the, which does the same comparison in ordinary speech.
examples: Just as the coach demanded loyalty, so he gave it.
Just as a garden needs weeding, so a budget needs pruning.
As the twig is bent, so grows the tree.
Just as athletes taper before a race, so too should writers rest before a deadline.
Just as the city rebuilt after the fire, so it will rebuild after the flood.
Just as a bad hire costs a year, so a good one pays for a decade.

entries.type: correlative (less is also a determiner, a pronoun, and a degree adverb; than is prepositional in less than me)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison, usually elliptical
entries.pattern: less [adjective/adverb] than [noun phrase/clause] · less [uncountable noun] than [noun phrase] · [verb] less than [noun phrase/clause] · less of a [noun] than [noun phrase] · fewer [countable noun] than [noun phrase/clause]
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair.
entries.meaning: Ranks the first item below the second — the mirror image of more … than. Careful American usage keeps less for uncountable amounts and fewer for things you can count one by one, though less with countables is everywhere in speech and on grocery-store signs.
examples: This route is less direct than the highway.
The repair cost less than we were quoted.
There are fewer seats than there were last season.
He seemed less interested than his partner did.
It took less effort than I expected.
The rewrite was less of a rescue than a demolition.

entries.type: correlative (more is also a determiner, a pronoun, and a degree adverb; than is prepositional in taller than me)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison, usually elliptical
entries.pattern: more [adjective/adverb] than [noun phrase/clause] · [short adjective]-er than [noun phrase/clause] · more [noun] than [noun phrase/clause] · [verb] more than [noun phrase/clause] · more [adjective] than [adjective] (two properties of one thing: more tired than hungry)
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair.
variants: -er … than (short adjectives: bigger than, sooner than)
entries.meaning: Ranks the first item above the second; the -er ending is the same correlative with the first half fused onto the adjective. When the second half is a bare pronoun, formal usage takes the subject form because a verb is understood — taller than I (am) — while ordinary speech says than me.
examples: The drive is more scenic than the flight.
She got here sooner than we did.
It rained more this June than in the last three Junes combined.
He knows more about the code than anyone left on the team.
The book is better than the movie.
There were more volunteers than we had jobs for.
By the third day she was more bored than homesick.

entries.type: correlative (so is also a coordinator and a degree adverb; as is also a preposition and a subordinator of time, reason, and manner)
entries.register: formal, old-fashioned (everyday American uses not as … as)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison, usually elliptical
entries.pattern: not so [adjective/adverb] as [noun phrase/clause] · not so [adjective] as to [verb] · not so much as [verb] (= not even) · not so much [X] as [Y]
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair.
variants: not so much as + verb (= not even)
entries.meaning: The older negative of as … as, kept alive in careful writing and in set phrases like not so fast and not so bad as all that. American English overwhelmingly prefers not as … as in speech, and the positive so … as (so good as this) is now archaic outside fixed expressions.
examples: The winter was not so harsh as the one before it.
He is not so young as he looks.
The rules are not so strict as people assume.
She was not so foolish as to sign it without reading it.
It's not so simple as it sounds.
She didn't so much as glance at the check.

entries.type: correlative (such is a determiner, not a conjunction — only as is; as is elsewhere a preposition and a subordinator of time, reason, and manner)
entries.clause: comparison clause of kind; introduces an example or a standard
entries.pattern: such [noun] as [noun phrase] · such a [singular noun] as [noun phrase] · such [noun] as [clause] · such … as to [verb] · [noun phrase], such as [examples], [rest of clause]
entries.punctuation: No comma before as when the such phrase restricts the noun. When such as introduces a nonessential list after an already complete noun phrase, set the list off with commas: citrus fruits, such as lemons and limes, keep for weeks.
entries.meaning: Points at a kind: such names the type and as introduces the example or standard that fixes it. Keep it apart from such … that, which measures a degree and reports a consequence.
examples: We don't stock such items as these anymore.
He had never faced such a decision as this one.
Bring such documents as the clerk asks for.
Root vegetables, such as carrots and parsnips, keep all winter.
Her tone was such as to end the discussion.
I've never heard such nonsense as came out of that meeting.

entries.type: correlative (neither half is the definite article; both are the Old English instrumental þy, and this the has no other use in the language)
entries.clause: paired comparative clauses — the first is subordinate, the second is the main clause
entries.pattern: The [comparative] [subject] [verb], the [comparative] [subject] [verb]. · The [comparative] [noun phrase], the [comparative] [clause]. (verb omitted in the first half: The higher the rate, …) · The more [noun] [clause], the more [noun] [clause]. · The [comparative], the [comparative]. (both verbs dropped: The sooner the better.)
entries.punctuation: Comma between the halves in the full-clause version: The more you practice, the easier it gets. Short verbless pairs normally drop it: The sooner the better.
entries.meaning: States that two quantities move together — change one and the other follows. The the here is not the article but a fossil of an old instrumental form meaning "by that much," which is why it can sit in front of a comparative.
examples: The more you practice, the easier it gets.
The longer we waited, the worse the line got.
The sooner the better.
The less he said, the more suspicious she became.
The higher the interest rate, the fewer people qualify.
The more people we invite, the more food we'll need.

entries.type: correlative (the same is article + adjective; only as is the conjunction, and that as is elsewhere a preposition — as a teacher — and a subordinator of time, reason, and manner; swapping in that turns the second half into a relative clause and changes the meaning)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison (identity), usually elliptical
entries.pattern: [X] is the same as [Y] · the same [noun] as [noun phrase] · the same [noun] as [clause] · [verb] the same as [clause] · the same [noun] that [relative clause] (identity of the one thing, not of the kind)
entries.punctuation: No comma before as.
variants: the same … that (relative clause — a different construction)
entries.meaning: Completes the comparison set: more … than ranks one thing above another, less … than below, as … as levels them, and the same … as claims they are of one kind. The choice between as and that after same decides what is being asserted — the same truck as we rented means one like it, the same truck that we rented means literally that vehicle. American speech drops the article freely in the standalone form (same as always), which is informal but not an error.
examples: Her handwriting looks the same as her mother's.
He ordered the same sandwich as I did.
The new lease has the same terms as the one it replaced.
Filing online works the same as mailing the form in.
Nothing in town tasted the same as it had before the fire.
Same as always — black coffee, no sugar.
She still drives the same truck that she bought in 2004.

entries.type: correlative (enough is also a determiner, a pronoun, and a degree adverb; the to here is the infinitive marker, not the preposition)
entries.clause: infinitival clause of degree and result
entries.pattern: [adjective/adverb] enough to [verb] · enough [noun] to [verb] · [adjective] enough for [noun] to [verb] · [verb] enough to [verb] · [adjective] enough that [clause]
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair.
variants: enough … that + clause (warm enough that we ate outside)
entries.meaning: Says the degree reaches the threshold the action requires — the positive counterpart of too … to. Mind the word order, which is unlike anything else in English: enough follows an adjective or adverb (old enough) but precedes a noun (enough chairs).
examples: She's old enough to vote.
We have enough chairs to seat forty.
He didn't run fast enough to catch the bus.
The ice was thick enough for the truck to cross.
The offer was good enough to take seriously.
It got warm enough that we ate on the porch.
He saved enough over two summers to pay for the first year.

entries.respell: SOH … az-too, uhz-tuh (the degree word so carries the stress; as to is unstressed and normally reduces)
entries.type: correlative (so is also a coordinator and a degree adverb; as to elsewhere is a two-word preposition meaning "regarding" — no word as to when)
entries.clause: infinitival clause of result
entries.pattern: so [adjective/adverb] as to [verb] · not so [adjective] as to [verb] · be so [adjective] as to [verb] (courtesy formula: be so kind as to) · such … as to [verb] (with a noun phrase)
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair.
entries.meaning: The compact, formal version of so … that: it names a degree and its consequence without building a second clause. Outside legal and academic prose most of its working life is spent in the fixed politeness formula would you be so kind as to.
examples: The margin was so narrow as to be meaningless.
Would you be so kind as to sign at the bottom?
His account was so detailed as to leave no doubt.
She was not so careless as to leave the door unlocked.
The evidence is so thin as to invite an appeal.
She spoke so softly as to be almost inaudible.

entries.type: correlative (so is also a coordinator — I was tired, so I left — and half of the purpose subordinator so that; that is also a complementizer, a relative pronoun, and a demonstrative)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of result
entries.pattern: so [adjective/adverb] that [clause] · so [adjective/adverb] [clause] (that dropped) · so much/many/little/few [noun] that [clause] · [verb] so much that [clause] · So [adjective] was [subject] that [clause] (formal inversion)
entries.punctuation: No comma before that. Do not confuse this pair with the purpose conjunction so that, where the two words form a single unit and are not split by an adjective — He left early so that he could beat the traffic.
entries.meaning: Measures a degree in the first half and reports its consequence in the second. So attaches to adjectives, adverbs, and quantity words; when the degree word needs to sit on a noun phrase instead, the pair becomes such … that.
examples: It was so hot that we gave up and went inside.
She spoke so quietly that nobody in back could hear.
There were so many applicants that they extended the deadline.
The line moved so slowly we left.
He had so little time that he skipped lunch.
So convincing was the demo that they signed on the spot.

entries.type: correlative (such is a determiner, not a conjunction — only that is; that is elsewhere a complementizer, a relative pronoun, and a demonstrative)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of result
entries.pattern: such a/an [adjective] [singular noun] that [clause] · such [adjective] [plural or uncountable noun] that [clause] · such [noun] [clause] (that dropped) · Such was [noun phrase] that [clause] (formal inversion)
entries.punctuation: No comma before that.
entries.meaning: The noun-phrase counterpart of so … that — the degree word attaches to a noun instead of an adjective. Watch where the article lands: such a good movie that… but so good a movie that….
examples: It was such a long meeting that two people walked out.
They had such bad luck that they stopped entering.
She showed such patience that the whole room calmed down.
It's such a small town that everyone knows your car.
Such was the noise that we had to shout to be heard.
He told such a good story nobody noticed the check had come.

entries.respell: TOO … too, tuh (the first too keeps its full vowel; the to reduces)
entries.type: correlative (too is also the additive adverb of me too and a bare intensifier — too loud; the to here is the infinitive marker, not the preposition)
entries.clause: infinitival clause of degree and result
entries.pattern: too [adjective/adverb] to [verb] · too [adjective] for [noun] to [verb] · too much/many [noun] to [verb] · [verb] too [adverb] to [verb] · only too [adjective] to [verb]
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair.
variants: only too … to (emphatic and positive: only too glad to help)
entries.meaning: Says the degree passes a limit, so the action does not happen — it carries a built-in negative that so … that does not. He was too tired to drive means he did not drive; He was so tired that he drove badly means he did.
examples: He was too tired to drive home.
The box is too heavy to lift by yourself.
She spoke too fast for me to follow.
There's too much going on to think straight.
It's too early to call the race.
I was only too glad to help.

entries.type: correlative (barely is also a plain degree adverb — barely enough; when is also an interrogative and a relative adverb)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: [subject] had barely [past participle] when [clause]. · Barely had [subject] [past participle] when [clause]. · [subject] had barely [past participle] before [clause]. · [subject] was barely [complement] when [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves. Fronting barely requires inversion of subject and auxiliary; leaving it after the subject does not.
entries.meaning: Says the second event arrived before the first had finished settling. Of the three when pairs it is the most conversational, and Americans far more often leave barely in place after the subject than front it.
examples: We had barely sat down when the fire alarm went off.
Barely had the game started when the rain came.
She had barely hung up when he called back.
I'd barely opened the box when I saw the crack.
The plane had barely left the gate when they turned it around.
We were barely through the first song before the power cut out.

entries.type: correlative (hardly is also a plain degree adverb — hardly anyone; when is also an interrogative and a relative adverb)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Hardly had [subject] [past participle] when [clause]. · [subject] had hardly [past participle] when [clause]. · [subject] had hardly [past participle] before [clause]. · [subject] was hardly [complement] when [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves. Fronted hardly requires subject-auxiliary inversion — Hardly had we left, never Hardly we had left.
entries.meaning: Marks two events as nearly simultaneous, the first barely complete before the second began. Its second half is when or before — pairing it with than is the classic crossover error with no sooner … than.
examples: Hardly had she left when the phone rang.
We had hardly unpacked when the neighbors came over.
Hardly had the words left his mouth when he regretted them.
The ink was hardly dry when the terms changed.
I had hardly started the engine before the light turned red.
Hardly had the season opened when their best pitcher went down.

entries.type: correlative (sooner is the comparative of the adverb soon, which is why the pair takes than; than on its own is prepositional in than me)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: No sooner had [subject] [past participle] than [clause]. · [subject] had no sooner [past participle] than [clause]. · No sooner was [subject] [complement] than [clause]. · No sooner does [subject] [verb] than [clause]. (present-tense habitual)
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves. Fronted no sooner forces inversion of the subject and the auxiliary.
variants: none — no sooner … when is a frequent error; the second half is always than
entries.meaning: The tightest of the immediate-sequence pairs: the second event follows so fast it seems to interrupt the first. Sooner is a comparative, which is exactly why the pair takes than, unlike hardly, scarcely, and barely, which take when or before.
examples: No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm went off.
No sooner had she fixed one bug than two more appeared.
He had no sooner signed the lease than he lost the job.
No sooner was the tent up than the wind knocked it flat.
No sooner had the news broken than the stock dropped.
No sooner does one machine come back online than another goes down.

entries.type: correlative (scarcely is also a plain degree adverb — scarcely audible; when is also an interrogative and a relative adverb)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: Scarcely had [subject] [past participle] when [clause]. · [subject] had scarcely [past participle] when [clause]. · Scarcely [noun phrase] had [past participle] when [clause]. · [subject] had scarcely [past participle] before [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves; inversion is required whenever scarcely is fronted.
entries.meaning: The bookish member of the group — identical in meaning to hardly … when, but rare in American speech and mostly confined to written narrative.
examples: Scarcely had the door closed when the arguing started.
He had scarcely finished speaking when the lights failed.
Scarcely had they reached the summit when the storm broke.
The town had scarcely recovered when the second flood came.
Scarcely a week had passed when the letter arrived.
The ship had scarcely cleared the harbor before the fog closed in.

entries.type: correlative (rather alone is a degree adverb — rather cold — and a corrective discourse marker — or rather; than is prepositional in than me)
entries.clause: coordinate elements; with a bare infinitive, an adverbial clause of preference
entries.pattern: [X] rather than [Y] · [verb] [X] rather than [Y] · Rather than [bare infinitive or -ing], [main clause]. · [subject] chose to [verb] rather than [bare infinitive] · [subject] would rather [bare infinitive] than [bare infinitive]
entries.punctuation: No comma when rather than joins two parallel elements inside a clause. When a rather than phrase is fronted, close it with a comma: Rather than argue, he left. A comma before a trailing rather than is optional and marks it as an afterthought.
variants: instead of (takes a noun or -ing only)
entries.meaning: Marks the first element as chosen and the second as rejected. It differs from instead of in what it can take: rather than accepts a bare infinitive (rather than wait), while instead of cannot (instead of waiting). Keep both sides in the same grammatical form.
examples: We took the train rather than the bus.
Rather than argue about it, he just paid the fee.
She'd call it a delay rather than a cancellation.
The change helps borrowers rather than banks.
He chose to resign rather than be fired.
Rather than raising prices, they cut the portion size.

entries.respell: wood-RA-thur … THAN, thuhn (usually heard as I'd RA-thur … thuhn)
entries.type: correlative (rather alone is a degree adverb and a corrective discourse marker; than is prepositional in than me; would rather is a fixed modal idiom that becomes a correlative only when than arrives)
entries.clause: coordinate bare-infinitive phrases; with a new subject, a clause of unreal preference
entries.pattern: [subject] would rather [bare infinitive] than [bare infinitive] · [subject]'d rather [bare infinitive] than [bare infinitive] · Would [subject] rather [bare infinitive] than [bare infinitive]? · [subject] would rather have [past participle] than [past participle] · [subject] would rather [new subject] [past-form verb] (unreal: I'd rather you didn't)
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the pair.
entries.meaning: States a personal preference between two actions, both in the bare infinitive — no to on either side. When the preference is about someone else's behavior, the second half becomes a clause with a past-tense verb that carries present meaning: I'd rather you didn't smoke.
examples: I'd rather walk than wait for the shuttle.
She'd rather pay the fine than go to traffic school.
Would you rather meet Tuesday than Thursday?
I'd rather you didn't mention it to him.
He'd rather have stayed home than sat through that.
They'd sooner close the store than sell it.

entries.type: correlative (an inverted present subjunctive of be plus the ordinary coordinator or; the same fossilized inversion drives were it not for and had I known)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition (= whether it is X or Y)
entries.pattern: Be it [X] or [Y], [main clause]. · [main clause], be it [X] or [Y]. · Be it [X], [Y], or [Z], [main clause]. (three or more) · Be they [X] or [Y], [main clause]. (plural subject) · Be it ever so [adjective], [main clause]. (fixed: be it ever so humble)
entries.punctuation: Set the whole be it phrase off with a comma wherever it sits, fronted or trailing — unlike most subordinate halves in this file, it keeps its comma in both positions, because it comments on the main clause rather than restricting it. No comma between the halves.
entries.meaning: Says the main claim holds whichever of the listed possibilities turns out to be true — the compressed, inverted form of whether it is X or Y. The verb is the bare subjunctive be, never is, and the inversion is what marks the clause as concessive rather than as a command: Be it rain or shine, the market opens at six.
examples: Be it rain or shine, the market opens at six.
Every application gets the same review, be it from a freshman or a full professor.
Be it a typo or a lie, the number in that filing is wrong.
The fee is the same, be it one night or seven.
Be they citizens or visitors, everyone waits in the same line.
Be it ever so humble, the cabin was warm and the roof held.

entries.type: correlative frame (between is a preposition, not a conjunction — only and is, and that and is the ordinary coordinator; between is also an adverb in in between)
entries.clause: none — it pairs two noun phrases inside a prepositional phrase, coordinating without creating a clause
entries.pattern: between [X] and [Y] · between [number] and [number] · the difference between [X] and [Y] · between [-ing phrase] and [-ing phrase] · Between [X] and [Y], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves. When a between … and phrase opens the sentence as an adverbial of cause, close it with a comma: Between the traffic and the rain, we were an hour late.
variants: among (three or more not treated pairwise)
entries.meaning: Fixes two endpoints — of a range, a relationship, or a comparison — and and is the only legal second half. Between X to Y is always an error. Between is fine with more than two items when each is being paired against the others (trade between the fifty states), but a plain list of three usually wants among.
examples: The store is open between nine and six.
Somewhere between Tulsa and Amarillo, the radio died.
What's the difference between a lease and a rental agreement?
Between the traffic and the rain, we missed the first act.
The bill runs between forty and fifty dollars a month.
Between fixing the roof and replacing the water heater, the savings are gone.

entries.type: correlative frame (both halves are prepositions, not conjunctions; the to here is the preposition, not the infinitive marker of too … to)
entries.clause: none — it pairs two noun phrases as the endpoints of a range or a path
entries.pattern: from [X] to [Y] · from [time] to [time] · from [X] through [Y] (inclusive) · [verb] from [place] to [place] · everything from [X] to [Y] (spread of kinds)
entries.punctuation: No comma between the halves. Never mix the words with a dash: write from 1999 to 2003 or 1999–2003, but not from 1999–2003.
variants: from … through (inclusive of the last unit)
entries.meaning: Marks a starting point and an ending point — in space, in time, or across a spread of kinds. Where between … and names two endpoints as a bounded interval, from … to traces extent or movement across it, and only from … to can describe a path.
examples: The shop is open from ten to six.
We drove from Denver to Santa Fe in a day.
The class covers everything from soldering to firmware.
Prices dropped from thirty dollars to nineteen.
She read the report from cover to cover.
The permit runs from June through September.

entries.type: correlative (if is also a complementizer in indirect questions — ask if he's home; then is an adverb, not a conjunction, which is exactly why it can be dropped)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition
entries.pattern: If [clause], then [main clause]. · If [clause], [main clause]. (then dropped — the ordinary form) · [main clause] if [clause]. (no comma, no then) · If not [X], then [Y].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the if clause when it comes first, whether or not then follows; the comma goes before then, never after it. When the if clause trails the main clause, use no comma — and then is not available in that order.
entries.meaning: One of only two correlatives whose second half can be dropped freely — the other is though … yet. Then adds no meaning, only logical sharpness, which is why it survives in mathematics, contracts, and code and is usually left out of ordinary prose. Examples 6 and 7 show the two forms that lose it: the ordinary comma'd version with then dropped, and the reversed order, where the trailing if clause takes no comma and cannot take then at all.
examples: If it rains, then we'll move the ceremony inside.
If the card is declined, then the order is canceled automatically.
If you're not going, then neither am I.
If that's the best offer, then I'll pass.
If not this week, then sometime next month.
If the meeting runs long, I'll text you.
Call the front desk if the heat doesn't come on.

entries.type: correlative (though is also a plain concessive subordinator — though it rained, we went — and a sentence-final adverb meaning "however": Nice, though.; yet is also one of the seven coordinators and a time adverb — not yet)
entries.register: formal and old-fashioned in the paired form — modern American keeps though and drops yet; the full pair survives mainly in sermons, legal prose, and older literature
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Though [clause], yet [main clause]. · Although [clause], yet [main clause]. · Though [clause], still [main clause]. · Though [adjective or noun phrase], yet [main clause]. (verbless first half) · Though [clause], [main clause]. (yet dropped — the ordinary modern form) · [main clause], though [clause]. (no yet available in this order)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted though clause whether or not yet follows; the comma goes before yet, never after it. Concession is the one place where reversing the order does not remove the comma — a trailing though clause keeps it, because it contrasts with the main clause rather than restricting it: Nobody would pay to fix it, though the roof leaked all spring. Compare the trailing if clause of if … then, which takes none.
variants: in current American English the second half is normally just left out
entries.meaning: Concedes a point in the first half and asserts the main claim anyway in the second, with yet marking the turn. The pairing is a survival: Old and Middle English routinely propped up a fronted concessive clause with a resumptive adverb, and yet is what is left of that. A modern editor will usually cut it as redundant — though has already done the concessive work — so use the full pair only when you want the deliberate weight of older prose.
examples: Though the evidence was thin, yet the jury convicted.
Although the company posted record sales, yet the stock fell.
Though she had every reason to walk out, yet she stayed to the end.
Though young, yet he ran the whole shop by himself.
Though the roof leaked all spring, still nobody would pay to fix it.
Though the roof leaked all spring, nobody would pay to fix it.
Nobody would pay to fix it, though the roof leaked all spring.

entries.respell: WUT-with … and, uhn (some Americans end with in /θ/; the stress sits on what)
entries.type: correlative frame (what with is a compound preposition — only and is a conjunction, and it is the ordinary coordinator; what elsewhere is an interrogative and a relative pronoun)
entries.clause: none — a prepositional adjunct of cause, so both halves take noun phrases or -ing phrases
entries.pattern: What with [X] and [Y], [main clause]. · What with [-ing phrase] and [-ing phrase], [main clause]. · What with [X], [Y], and [Z], [main clause]. (three or more causes) · What with [X] and [Y] and all, [main clause]. · [main clause], what with [X] and [Y].
entries.punctuation: The whole what with phrase is set off from the main clause by a comma, wherever it sits in the sentence.
entries.meaning: Piles up two or more causes as an informal explanation, usually for something that went wrong. It takes nouns and -ing phrases and never a finite clause — what with the baby crying, not what with the baby cried.
examples: What with the traffic and the rain, we got there an hour late.
What with work and the new baby, we haven't unpacked a box.
She's exhausted, what with the move and the audit and everything.
What with the layoffs and the hiring freeze, morale is shot.
We skipped the trip, what with gas prices and the car making that noise.
What with the dog barking and the neighbors hammering, I couldn't hear a word.

entries.type: correlative (where is the subordinator; there is a resumptive adverb, not a conjunction, which is exactly why it can be dropped — the same arrangement as the then of if … then)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of place, routinely generalized to circumstance
entries.pattern: Where [clause], there [main clause]. · Where [clause], there [verb] [subject]. (inverted main clause) · Where [clause], there [main clause] also. · Where [clause], [main clause]. (there dropped — the ordinary modern form) · [main clause] where [clause]. (no there available in this order) · Wherever [clause], there [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted where clause whether or not there follows; the comma goes before there, never after it. Reversed, the trailing where clause takes no comma and cannot take there at all. One look-alike to resist: in Where there's smoke, there's fire the second there is the dummy subject of there is, not the resumptive adverb, and the pair is doing the same job by accident.
entries.meaning: Names a place, or more often a kind of situation, in the first half and asserts what holds in it in the second, with there pointing back at the where clause. Like the then of if … then, the there adds emphasis rather than meaning and is normally dropped in modern prose; when it is kept, formal style often inverts the main clause behind it — there will your heart be also.
examples: Where the road ends, there the trail begins.
Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Where the water runs deepest, there the current is slowest.
Where the statute is silent, there custom governs.
Where two or three inspectors disagree, there the paperwork multiplies.
Where the tax was actually collected, the roads got paved.
Weeds grow thickest where the shade is deepest.
